title: Lead with the takeaway
body: In status updates, put the conclusion in the first sentence, then the supporting detail. Busy stakeholders read the first line and skim the rest — bury the takeaway and it gets lost.

title: The illusion of communication
body: The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place.
author: George Bernard Shaw

title: The serial interrupter
body: A senior engineer keeps talking over others in team meetings. What is the highest-leverage first move?

options.label: Call it out publicly in the next meeting
Talk to them privately, describe the specific pattern, and ask what is driving it
Restructure the meeting so they always present last
Ignore it — it will resolve itself

explanation: A private, specific conversation preserves their dignity and usually surfaces the real cause (anxiety, habit, or not feeling heard) faster than a public correction or a structural workaround.

title: Read it as your harshest critic
body: Before sending critical feedback in writing, reread it imagining the recipient forwarding it to someone else. If that would embarrass you, it is not ready to send.

title: The status report that hid the truth
body: A team lead wrote "tracking with minor risk" for three weeks straight while a launch date quietly slipped. When it finally broke, leadership was angrier about the report than the delay. Ambiguity, under real stakes, reads as dishonesty.

title: Ask what you don't know
body: In your next 1:1, ask one question you genuinely don't already know the answer to — then let the silence sit for five seconds before filling it.

title: Match the channel to the message
body: A correction or hard truth belongs in a call or in person, not Slack. Recognition can go in public; correction almost never should.

title: Silence is a tool, not a gap to fill
body: In a debate-heavy meeting, waiting a beat before responding to a hot take gets you better information than jumping in immediately — and signals you actually heard it.

title: What isn't said
body: The most important thing in communication is hearing what isn't said.
author: Peter Drucker

title: Numbers need a comparison
body: "We shipped 40 features" means nothing on its own. "...versus 25 last quarter" or "...against a target of 50" is what turns a number into information.

title: The update that trained people to stop reading
body: A manager wrote "tracking, no major updates" in the weekly report for months. The one week everything actually fell apart, nobody had the context to help — they had all stopped reading. A boring update is still an update.

title: Write for the person who skims
body: Bold the one sentence that actually matters and bullet the rest. Assume nobody reads past the first two lines unless those two lines have already earned it.

title: A basic question, asked in public
body: A junior engineer asks a question in a public Slack channel that reveals a gap in a basic concept. What is the best response?

options.label: Answer privately only, and leave the public message unanswered
Answer plainly in the same public channel, with no comment on the knowledge gap
"Good question!" in public, then DM the real answer
Wait to see if someone else answers it

explanation: Answering plainly and publicly signals that no question is a dumb question — which is exactly what gets a team to keep asking things early, before they become expensive mistakes.

title: Explain a decision in two sentences
body: Take a decision you made recently and explain it to someone outside your team in two sentences. If you can't, you understand it less well than you think.

title: Calibrate your certainty language
body: "I think" and "I'm confident" are not interchangeable. Using "I'm sure" for a guess costs you trust the first time you turn out to be wrong.
